To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (R-fMRI), which measures low-frequency spontaneous fluctuations in blood oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) fMRI signals, can be used to construct maps of functional connectivity in the human brain; 2) the resulting maps, or functional connectomes, exhibit consistent patterns of positive and negative connectivity between brain regions, and consistent loci of individual variability; 3) age and sex are significant determinants of functional connectivity; 4) R-fMRI
resting-state functional MRI can be used to map the functional connectome in a consistent manner across subjects, and that this connectome is highly reproducible across sites and individuals.

resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) can reveal functional connectivity in the brain, and that the functional connectivity of the brain is reproducible across individuals, centers, and imaging platforms.

understanding the brain as a complex system, and how it changes over the life course.
understanding human brain function. We are interested in how the brain functions as a system, and
understanding the human brain and how it works.

resting state fMRI is a promising approach to the discovery science of brain structure and function.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human connectome is a highly reproducible, yet highly variable, feature of the brain.
the functional connectome of the brain is highly reproducible across individuals and centers.

R-fMRI can be used to study the human brain at a systems level.
